full_judgment:
ABM KhairuI Haque J: This Rule, under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, was issued at the instance of the petitioner, calling upon the opposite parties to show cause, as to, why certain observations made by the Sessions Judge, Jhalakati, in his judgment and order dated 11-10-1998, in Criminal Appeal No.4 of 1998, setting aside the judgment and order dated 5-7-1998, passed by the petitioner, as the concerned Magistrate, in Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1998, should not be expunged and also to show cause as to why the First Class Magisterial power of the petitioner should not be restored with effect from 11-10-1999, the date of withdrawal of his such power by the order dated 11-10-1999, passed by the Establishment Division, Government of Bangladesh (Annexure-A to the petition). 

 2. The case of the petitioner, in brief, is that he was posted at Jhalakati as a Magistrate, First Class, Jhalakati 'Kha' area and while he was conducting his Court on 5-7-1998, at about 16-30 hours, one of the accused, namely, Mohammad Ali Khan, was dozing in a chair in his Court-room and was yawning which caused interruption in the proceedings of the Court, as such, the petitioner drew a proceeding under section 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, convicting the said accused under section 228 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to pay a fine of Taka 200.00, in default to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of seven days. Against the said order of conviction and sentence dated 5-7-1998, passed by the petitioner, the convict filed a criminal appeal before the Sessions Judge, Jhalakati, being Criminal Appeal No.4 of 1998 and the learned Sessions Judge by his judgment and order dated 11-10-1998, allowed the appeal and set aside the order of conviction and sentence. But in course of his judgment, the learned Judge made not only certain uncharitable observations about the competency of the petitioner as a Magistrate First Class, but also recommended withdrawal of his First Class Magisterial power. In due course, the Government by its order dated 11-10-1998 withdrew his First Class Magisterial power. 

 8. In disposing of this criminal miscellaneous case under section 561A of the Code, we intend to discuss in brief about the purpose of section 228 of the Penal Code and the procedure for its enforcement, because, in the instant case, neither the learned Magistrate nor the learned Sessions Judge, appreciated the intent and purport of these provisions. 

 The said provision together with the schedule provides for the forum and the manner of trial of all offences under the Penal Code. In this connection it must be borne in mind that the Code of Criminal Procedure does not permit trial of any offence under the Penal Code except by a Court. The eighth column of the Second Schedule provides that the offences referred to in section 228 of the Penal Code is triable in the Court in which the offence is committed subject to the provisions of Chapter XXXV. It is therefore apparent that an offence under section 228 of the Penal Code cannot be tried except by a Court and under the provisions of section 28 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court itself must be the Court which has been interrupted or insulted. It is therefore manifest that section 228 of the Penal Code wields the Court with extraordinary power of being the complainant, the prosecution and the judge. The purpose in wielding the Court with such power is to maintain and uphold the dignity and prestige of Courts of justice. The reason is, in the words of ID Dua, J in the case of Captain Gurbakhsb Singhvs State, AIR 1960 (Punjab) 211. 

 11. In the instant case, the certified copy of the order sheet of the Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1998, in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Jhalakati, 'Kha' Area (Annexure-C2 to the petition) shows that on 5-7-1998 at about 16-30 hours in the afternoon, while the petitioner was considering a bail petition as a presiding Magistrate, in GR No. 53 of 1998, one Md Ali Khan, an accused, was dozing on a chair in the Court-room and was yawning from time to time. The learned Magistrate considered this conduct of the said offender as an interruption in his judicial work, as such, by his order No.1 dated 5-7-1998 he took cognizance against him under section 228 of the Penal Code. But the offender pleaded guilty and begged to be excused when he was asked to show any cause as to why he should not be convicted. But instead, the learned Magistrate proceeded against him under section 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and convicted him under section 228 of the Penal Code sentencing him to pay a fine of Taka 200.00 with default order. On appeal, the learned Sessions Judge set aside the conviction on two grounds. Firstly, the conduct of the offender did not constitute an insult or interruption to the judicial proceedings, and secondly, the learned Magistrate did not follow the proper procedure in summarily convicting the offender. 

 12. It should clearly be understood that contempt is committed not only by hurling abusive language to the Presiding Judge or by active interruption of the proceeding of the Court it can also be committed by the manner and conduct of the offender. A language which may otherwise be inoffensive, if spoken in a temperative manner, may become objectionable constituting an offence of contempt if blurted out in a disrespectful way. Similarly, the conduct of a person in the normal circumstances may otherwise be unobjectionable but if it is performed in a particular way or repeated in a distasteful manner in presence of a judicial officer while he is performing his judicial function, in spite of his disapproval of his such egregious behaviour, may become highly improper, constituting punishable contempt. It all, however, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the facts as emerge from the order sheet show that the offender though an accused, dozed of in his chair and also yawned from time to time but when charged with the offence of contempt promptly begged to be excused. The facts do not show that he was at all warned of his conduct and that in defiance of such warning he continued to doze and yawn recklessly and wilfully with intent to show disrespect and also to interrupt the proceedings of the Court. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, when the offender begged to be excused, the matter ought to have been dropped. 

 Besides, the status of the offender as Chairman of the Union Parishad appears to weigh with him. But the status of an offender is irrelevant in deciding the case under section 228 of the Penal Code. Rather, higher the status of a person, the more responsible conduct and behaviour is expected of him. 

 15. Let us now turn our eyes to the procedure adopted by the learned Magistrate in proceeding with a case under section 228 of the Penal Code. 

 "481(1). In every such case the Court shall record the facts constituting the offence, with the statement (if any) made by the offender, as well as the finding and sentence. 

 20. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that because of the observations and the recommendation made by the learned Sessions Judge, the Government in exercise of its power under section 41 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, by a notification dated 16-10-1999 (Annexure-A to the petition) withdrew the First Class Magisterial power of the petitioner. He submits that in making such unnecessary observations and recommendation, the learned Sessions Judge went beyond his jurisdiction as an appellate Court causing gross miscarriage of justice on this petitioner as a First Class Magistrate although there was no allegation of misconduct against him, as such, he prays that the observations and recommendation should be expunged for ends of justice. 

 21. We have gone through the relevant portions of the judgment in appeal. The observations about the performance of the petitioner as a Magistrate were not at all necessary in disposing of the appeal. It was rather uncalled for. The law has provided the forum of appeal and revision within the framework of the Code of Criminal Procedure to eliminate errors at every stage of judicial proceedings but the higher Court should not readily admonish a subordinate judicial officer for his lapse unless such error is so gross or perverse that the interest of the administration of justice requires such admonition. It appears that in the instant case, the learned Sessions Judge was swayed with emotion so much so that he not only made certain uncharitable observations about the performance of the petitioner as a Magistrate but also recommended withdrawal of his First Class Magisterial power with copies to the concerned authorities. 

 22. A District and Sessions Judge is the principal judicial officer in an Administrative District. Being a senior judicial officer, a District and Sessions Judge is expected to exercise sufficient self-restraint not to permit himself to be swayed or led away by impulse, in order to uphold the dignity of his important office. He should not, as in this case, being over exuberant do something which was not at all necessary and specially when his action is likely to prejudices another judicial officer even though subordinate. 

 23. In the instant case, the learned Sessions Judge after setting aside the order of conviction made the following observations: 

 25. This conduct on the part of the learned Sessions Judge in choosing to term/address the learned Magistrate as an 'accused' when he was not even a party in the appeal, was wholly inappropriate and preposterous. It only highlights his own emotion which was not expected of a senior judicial officer like him. In this connection, it should also be borne in mind that in disposing of an appeal or revision or any other matter, the superior Court evaluates the judgment and order of the subordinate Court but not the concerned subordinate judicial officer. Besides, even if the learned Sessions Judge takes a view that the Magisterial power of the petitioner should be withdrawn, he ought to have given him an opportunity commensurate with the age old principle of audi alteram partem, to explain his position before making any comment on his performance and recommending the withdrawal of his Magisterial power. It is unfortunate that the learned Sessions Judge who did not hesitate to make uncalled for remarks for the lapses of the learned Magistrate, himself did not observe the most cardinal principle of law. Failure of the learned Sessions Judge, in this case, to give an opportunity to the learned Magistrate, would render his comments and his recommendation invalid and non est in the eye of law.
